strengths: Addresses an important deployment problem. Combining density-ratio estimation with weighted score calibration is an intuitive, potentially useful approach that does not require retraining the monitored classifier.

The evaluation includes 959 model–dataset combinations and 36,557 production chunks across five classification tasks and five model families. PAPE achieves the best results on all six aggregate measures in Table 1; compared with IW, MASTE decreases from 1.05 to 0.99 for accuracy, 1.07 to 1.00 for AUROC, and 1.06 to 0.91 for F1.

IW using the same density-ratio estimator and unweighted CBPE provide useful component comparisons. Standard-error-normalized evaluation and analysis across performance-change magnitudes are relevant to practical monitoring.

Public datasets, explicit temporal splits, and a repository link support reproducibility. The discussion candidly acknowledges concept shift, insufficient support overlap, and finite-sample limitations. No material research-ethics concern is evident.
weaknesses: The central algorithm and proof do not establish the claimed applicability to any performance metric. Equations (1)–(2) cover expectations of per-observation contributions, such as accuracy, but do not directly cover F1 or AUROC. F1 requires nonlinear aggregation, while AUROC requires ranking or pairwise treatment; the actual estimators for these two headline metrics are unspecified. Equation (4) also incorrectly equates expected absolute label residual with absolute conditional calibration error. These gaps undermine the claimed theoretical support.

Important implementation details are missing from the manuscript: the density-ratio classifier, calibration model and loss, preprocessing, hyperparameters, and treatment of extreme weights. Algorithm 1 fits the domain classifier and evaluates it on the same reference observations without explaining safeguards against overfitting. Although code is linked, the supplied methodological description is insufficient to determine precisely what produced the reported results.

The many evaluation cases all derive from related Folktables tasks and populations. Temporal changes need not satisfy the assumed invariant label conditional, and there are no controlled experiments with known covariate shifts or density ratios to isolate the proposed mechanism. The sample-size analysis covers only one selected case, limiting conclusions about robustness.

Statistical support for superiority is incomplete. The reported Wilcoxon p = 0.0 does not specify the testing unit or handling of dependence among chunks, models, and shared datasets; confidence intervals and variability across runs are absent. ATC and DoC are also extended to F1 and AUROC without establishing that these adaptations are competitive. The IW comparison is more persuasive, but its relatively modest average improvements warrant clearer uncertainty reporting.

Originality and scope need sharper positioning. The theoretical argument largely combines conditional expectation with established importance-weighted calibration, without clearly distinguishing the contribution from prior work such as [11]. The abstract additionally claims reliance only on predictions and no assumptions about shift, whereas Algorithm 1 requires input features and the justification requires covariate shift and support overlap. Together with the missing metric definitions and implementation details, these issues outweigh the promising empirical results.
